WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over lending money

When you're asked, it's hard to decline; if you lend, you're anxious about whether it will come back, and afraid the relationship itself might break. Being torn over lending and borrowing money is a decision where feeling for the other person and the desire to protect yourself collide head-on. This page introduces, before lending or not lending, perspectives for thinking about a line that protects both the relationship and the money, and the tarot cards that reflect those perspectives.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

Being torn over whether to lend money is a problem of the relationship more than of money itself. If you decline, will you be thought cold? If you lend and it doesn't come back, will you end up resenting the other person? Both fears stop your judgment. You also tend to decide on the feeling of wanting to help alone, while the amount requested and the reason remain vague. Lent money continues to create tension within the relationship until it returns. Start by looking separately at the depth of your relationship with the other person, the size of the amount, and how certain the reason is. On top of that, whether it is an amount you could lose without it affecting your life is the realistic dividing line.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

The key to sorting this out is not to make it a two-way choice between lending and declining. There are middle ways to choose: lend a smaller amount, help with only part of it, or be of help in a form other than money. If you lend, putting the timing and method of repayment into words and keeping a record helps protect the relationship. It may feel hard to say, but lending while things are vague is more of a burden on the relationship later. And if you use as your own standard whether it is an amount you could give up on even if it didn't come back, the ceiling you can lend comes into view. If you decline, too, communicating your own circumstances briefly, rather than explaining your reasons at length, tends to give less offense.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over lending and borrowing money, cards that reflect the balance of giving, fairness, and the relationship after lending can offer useful clues.

The Six of Pentacles depicts a person with means sharing with someone in need, showing the balance between the side that gives and the side that receives.

Justice is a stance of judging things with a fair line, without being swept along by feeling.

The Five of Cups reflects regret over what was lost, and the lingering strain left in a relationship. Check whether the card you drew leans toward giving or toward drawing a line, and confirm how your feelings are tilting.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. Is the amount requested within a range that wouldn't affect your life even if it didn't come back? Are the other person's reason for asking and their outlook for repayment concrete? If you lend, how is this relationship likely to change? If you decline, what would be the most sincere way to communicate it? Is there a way you could help other than with money? Deciding with both feeling and reality set side by side protects both the other person and you.

CARDS

Cards connected to this decision

  • Six of Pentacles

    The figure of sharing, and balance. A card that asks whether the giving side has room to spare.

  • Justice

    Shows a stance of judging with a fair line, without being swept along by feeling.

  • Five of Cups

    Regret over what was lost. It reflects the lingering strain in a relationship after lending.

  • Five of Swords

    A relationship where winning and losing remain. The danger of lending and borrowing turning into conflict.

  • Four of Pentacles

    A stance of protecting your own share. A perspective for discerning the ceiling you can lend.

Lend, or not lend? Why not think about a line that values both the money and the relationship?
